row.name: Southeast Face
row.overview: A big, imposing wall above the lake that was not climbed before the early 1960s. The first party, all experienced Valley climbers, discovered many squared holds linking broken crack systems.
row.approach: Cecile Lake is the jumping-off point. A well-worn path leads to Minaret Lake; beyond it the way turns rougher and fainter. Expect snow cover on the stretch between Iceberg Lake and the foot of the route.

row.name: South Face
row.overview: Twelve pitches. P1 (5.4): groove, right to a knobby wall, spike belay. P2 (5.6): detached-block corner and cracks past an overlap to an alcove. P3 (5.6): left wall, ramp, crack, slab. P4 (5.6): crack, chimney crack, left-facing corner, nuts under the Slot. P5 (5.8): the Slot. P6-P7 (5.7): crack, then pinnacles and a right-facing corner. P8 (5.7+): intricate, with a 2.5 Friend placement in a pocket. P9 (5.6): furrowed face with sparse gear. P10-P11 (5.6): flake crack to a ledge with a dead tree, then the orange face. P12: easy to the summit ridge.

row.name: Traveler Buttress
row.overview: Four pitches at the Leap. A #4 Camalot set deep in the pitch-two offwidth crack protects it well, though two #4s are what most parties like; that offwidth is the crux, and it has a notorious reputation. Pitch one's serrated crack (5.7) has a brief flaring crux (5.8) high up, just above a ledge that would crush ankles. The final stretch is a dike hike, at fourth class up to easy fifth class.

row.name: Grizzly Couloir
row.overview: The widest and westernmost of the gullies seen on the peak's north face, and held up as the finest snow line of the whole range. Compared with a rival gully nearby it sheds less stone, and its condition can be checked from many summits north of it.
row.approach: Start at the Grizzly trailhead and follow the easy trail up to Grizzly Lake; most of it is fairly flat and the route is hard to lose. Circle the lake, then climb talus to the big snow couloir that drops to the right of the summit. Snow climbing begins somewhere above 12,600 feet depending on conditions. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
row.descent_text: The couloir tops out a short scramble from the summit and steepens as you climb, to around 45 to 50 degrees near the top. Either walk down the west slopes to the road, or glissade and downclimb the couloir with great care. Rocks fall from the cliffs on either side, so wear a helmet. A fall high up could slide a long way, though the angle eases a lot near the bottom. Check the avalanche forecast first.

row.name: East Ridge
row.description: Long grassy ridge in the remote eastern San Juans; mileage depends heavily on how far a vehicle can drive up the Stewart Creek road.

row.name: West Ridge
row.description: Short, mostly walking ascent along the Continental Divide ridge from the pass, with a bit of rocky stepping near the top.

row.name: North Face Variation
row.overview: Straighter and technically tougher than another line on this face; the rock is mostly good. About 1,000 feet of 4th class up slabs leads to the upper headwall, where many options exist. The left side looks easier, getting harder and steeper toward the right. The rock higher up may be very good.

row.name: North Face Couloirs
row.approach: From Breckenridge, take Spruce Creek Road to the Mohawk Lakes trailhead, parking as high as the road allows, then follow the trail past the abandoned mining works to Lower and Upper Mohawk Lakes. The route is the pair of couloirs on the right side of the north face; it is easiest to pass the lakes on their south ends to avoid marsh on the north. The meadow ends at the foot of the face, and the final climb to its base is a long, steady uphill.
row.descent_text: Descend as for the peak itself, by the east ridge. Cornices overhang the west ridge above the route.

row.name: Northeast Ridge
row.description: Rocky ridge scramble that is normally combined with North Apostle.

row.name: South Ridge and Couloir
row.description: Trail to Cathedral Lake, then a loose gully and ridge scramble to the summit above Aspen; rockfall and late-season loose scree are the main concerns.

row.name: West Face (White Couloir)
row.description: Steep couloir and west-face scrambling reached from the Maroon Lake area; very loose rock makes rockfall a serious hazard, so helmets and small parties matter.
